content:
Quick answer: Plan the journey inside the hospital as well as the journey there. Check the appointment instructions, ask about access or communication support early, and confirm transport and parking arrangements before travelling. NHS patient transport and travel-cost help have separate eligibility rules. Bring medicines information and questions, and tell the clinic promptly if you cannot attend.

Pain, fatigue and difficulty getting up from a chair can make a short consultation a demanding day. This guide is about practical preparation for adults with arthritis and people supporting them. It cannot confirm your eligibility for transport, promise a particular adjustment or replace instructions for a test or procedure.

Start with four checks on your appointment letter

  1. Where: check the actual site, building and department. A trust may run clinics at several locations.
  2. How: is this in person, by telephone or by video? If travelling is difficult, ask whether another format would meet your clinical needs. Do not assume it has changed until the service confirms.
  3. Preparation: look for instructions about medicines, eating, drinking, samples or tests. If unclear, ask the clinic before changing anything.
  4. Contact: save the booking number and find out who to contact about access needs, delays or cancellation.

NHS outpatient guidance advises allowing time for the visit and registering at the department named in your details. Some visits involve further tests or waiting. Do not assume the consultation slot is the whole hospital visit.

Ask for help with the parts you find difficult

Explain the actual barrier: a long walk from the entrance, steps, standing in a queue, low chairs, hearing your name called, reading letters or communicating in an appointment. Ask what the service can arrange and how it will record the request. Examples to discuss include an accessible route, a suitable chair, communication support, an interpreter or help finding the department. These are requests to plan together, not facilities every site necessarily has.

NHS Highland advises contacting the service on your letter in advance about accessibility and interpreter needs. In England, the Accessible Information Standard requires NHS and adult social care services to identify and meet disability-related information and communication needs. Ask for the support you need rather than struggling with an unsuitable format.

Ask a companion what help they can offer, with your agreement. That might be a lift, help at reception or taking notes. They do not need to answer for you unless you want that support. If you need someone to travel with you on patient transport, check whether an escort is authorised when booking.

Patient transport is different from help paying for travel

Non-emergency patient transport

The NHS transport guide says most people arrange their own journey, while some qualify for NHS-funded patient transport. Ask your healthcare team or local transport service for an assessment early. Explain medical support, mobility, cognitive or sensory needs and why available alternatives are unsuitable.

Having arthritis, being older or finding a bus journey difficult does not by itself confirm eligibility. NHS England's eligibility framework considers safety, medical needs, significant mobility needs and other defined circumstances, with local assessment. Do not apply England's framework as a universal UK booking rule. Ask your own health board or trust about local arrangements, the return journey, collection point and what to do if transport is late.

Help with travel costs

A refund scheme does not automatically book a vehicle, and qualifying for one kind of help does not confirm the other. Before paying for an expensive journey, ask which costs are eligible, whether advance agreement is required and which evidence to keep.

  • England: the Healthcare Travel Costs Scheme can cover reasonable costs for eligible referred NHS specialist care. Financial eligibility and referral conditions apply. Agree taxi use in advance; do not assume a taxi receipt guarantees reimbursement.
  • Scotland: NHS inform explains transport-cost help, including financial eligibility and additional arrangements in some areas. Ask the hospital before travel.
  • Wales: GOV.WALES explains necessary travel-cost help for eligible people receiving care under a consultant. Check the hospital's claiming process and evidence requirements.
  • Northern Ireland: nidirect describes the Hospital Travel Costs Scheme. Contact the hospital in advance if ordinary transport is impractical and ask whether your proposed arrangements are allowed.

Keep your appointment details, receipts and any eligibility evidence the hospital requests. If you cannot afford the journey upfront, ask about support before the day rather than assuming you must miss care. Community or voluntary transport may be another option; check availability, accessibility and charges directly.

Parking: check the site and the validation process

Look up the closest suitable entrance, drop-off point and accessible route. Check height limits or vehicle restrictions if relevant, how payment works and whether your vehicle registration must be entered at reception. Bring your Blue Badge if you have one, but check the site's process rather than assuming displaying it is enough.

In England, government NHS parking guidance includes free parking for valid Blue Badge holders attending as patients or visitors. It also defines a frequent-outpatient group. This is not a blanket exemption for every person with arthritis or every hospital visit. Check your eligibility and the local validation steps. Outside England, use the hospital or health board's current parking information.

Pack for the visit without overlooking test instructions

  • Appointment details, requested records and a list of questions.
  • An up-to-date medicines and allergies list, including bought products and supplements.
  • Glasses, hearing aids, communication aids and your usual mobility aid.
  • A charged phone and the clinic and transport contact details.
  • Medicines due during the day, kept safely, with a plan agreed with the team if the appointment affects their timing.
  • A drink or snack only if your preparation instructions allow it. Ask if fasting or fluid restrictions apply.

Do not stop or change a prescribed medicine because of this checklist. If instructions conflict with your usual medicine routine, ask the clinic or pharmacist to clarify before the visit. If you may have a procedure affecting your ability to drive, ask about the journey home in advance.

During the visit and before going home

Tell reception if you cannot remain in the waiting area or need to move, use the toilet or sit somewhere else, so you are not missed. Ask for help if pain or fatigue is becoming difficult. You do not have to follow a fixed movement timetable from an article.

Put your main concern first. Ask for explanations in words you understand, and for important instructions to be written down. Before leaving, check what happens next, who arranges tests or follow-up, how results will arrive and whom to contact if they do not. For the clinical assessment itself, see what to expect at a first rheumatology appointment.

If you cannot attend or something goes wrong

Contact the clinic promptly if illness, a flare or transport failure prevents attendance. Ask what to do next and whether an alternative is suitable. Do not assume a missed appointment is automatically rebooked, or that every hospital applies the same discharge rule.

For an unresolved practical problem, ask the service about its patient-support or feedback route. In England, PALS can help with NHS questions and concerns. Other UK nations have their own routes through the hospital, health board or HSC trust. A complaints service is not urgent clinical care.

Do not wait for a routine appointment if you develop sudden severe joint pain, swelling or difficulty moving a joint. The NHS advises urgent assessment for possible joint infection; fever is not always present. Use your GP or local urgent-care service. Call 999 for a life-threatening emergency.

Keep your appointment notes together

The blank appointment sheet gives you space for symptoms, medicines and questions to take with you. The sheets do not send your entries to this website and are not a treatment plan.

  • GP appointment symptom and medication tracker (PDF)
  • All symptom and flare printables

The blank sheets are awaiting separate clinical review. Follow your existing care plan and the urgent-help advice in this guide. Do not delay medical help to complete a record.
